articles.content: Kirk Franklin did not walk through The Jennifer Hudson Show’s spirit tunnel. He worked it. The Jennifer Hudson Show posted the walk to Instagram with one caption: “Show off those moves @kirkfranklin!” View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Jennifer Hudson Show (@jenniferhudsonshow) He was there to promote his new album, I Am What I Am , which comes out Friday, Oct. 30. It’s his 14th solo album, and he’s a 20-time Grammy winner. His song with Karen Clark Sheard, “Thank You For Everything,” is already out. It made its live TV debut at the 41st Stellar Gospel Music Awards. At a listening party in Atlanta on Oct. 12, according to Hot 100.9, Franklin said, “I’ve never done a double album before.” He described the TobyMac collaboration “It Gets Better” as “my attempt to find a space to talk about mental health,” and added, “I’ve had my own journey with anxiety and depression.” He also talked about changes in the Black church. “The Black church culture changed,” he said. “The church got rid of their choirs and the music was in a space that was not my strength.” He had advice for emerging artists, too. “Start off very true and build your audience slow,” he said. “Don’t ride the trends because you don’t know when they’re coming.”

articles.title_zh: 马刺新秀Tarris Reed Jr.受洗： “我从不想与主无关，到现在渴望为他而活”
articles.content: San Antonio Spurs rookie Tarris Reed Jr. got baptized days after making his NBA debut, and he posted the video to Instagram under two words: “Jesus Saves.” Reed, a 23-year-old center, was the No. 26 pick in this year’s draft out of UConn. Denver took him, and San Antonio acquired him in a trade. He debuted on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in a 116-104 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder. In the caption, Reed wrote that he got home late after his first NBA back-to-back and “got my first real glimpse of just how grueling the 82-game NBA season can be.” On the plane ride, he remembered it was Baptism Sunday at his church. “I texted Pastor Ed, and the rest was history LOL.” “It’s been on my heart for a while now to be baptized,” Reed wrote. “I wanted to publicly signify my union with Christ and what it means to walk in His grace, mercy, and NEWNESS OF LIFE!” He quoted Romans 6:4: “We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.” He also wrote about what he sees coming next. “The Lord has placed me in a unique position to help others come to know Christ and experience His life changing power,” he wrote. “To think that I went from wanting nothing to do with the Lord to now desiring to live for Him is something I never could have imagined. I never would have thought my life would look like this.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by TRJ (@iamtarrisreed) Reed is a St. Louis native who started his college career at Michigan, transferred to UConn after his sophomore year and was the Big East Sixth Man of the Year as a junior. In April, UConn lost the national title game to Michigan, and Reed went to Instagram afterward. “I’ve been wrestling with God about this all day” , he wrote in a post that week. “Losing the biggest game of my entire basketball career hurts,” he said. “I tend to be a perfectionist, but only Jesus was perfect.” He wrote that he felt Jesus put it on his heart to go to an Athletes in Action meeting and speak, even though he didn’t want to. He barely had time to prepare, so he told himself he would let the Holy Spirit speak through him. “That night, two of the women’s basketball players got baptized,” he wrote. “It’s not my will, it’s His.” His October post ended with “All glory to God!”

articles.title_zh: 破碎的系统保护贩运者，而不是女孩
articles.content: I’m often asked about the night I spent in a Southeast Asian jail alongside three young girls who had been exploited by sex traffickers. But the primary question isn’t about why I was in jail. Rather, why were those three girls in jail to begin with? Why them, and not the traffickers who had taken them from their families and sold them repeatedly for sex, turning their lives into a brutal nightmare? Why not the woman who had put tape over the mouth of the young girl so that the man who was raping her would not be disturbed by her screams. The system failed them. The brothel keeper was tipped off about their rescue operation, allowed to hide her crime, and told to dump the girls at a nearby bus stop. The police who should have rescued them instead arrested them on immigration charges. The trafficker walked free, while the girls were treated as criminals. As I sat with them that night, I longed for those girls to have never been taken to jail, much less a brothel. I wanted them to have always been at home with their families, going to school, and playing with their friends. I wanted them to have never been harmed in the first place. But the reality is, like millions of women and girls in our world today, they suffered the consequences of a broken justice system. And so, the reason I stayed with the girls is simply that the alternative was just too horrible. I preferred to be arrested myself rather than leave them vulnerable to further assault. But there’s an important detail to clarify: in the end, I did not need to stay the full night. Once it was clear I was not going away, the jailer himself took on the responsibility of assuring their safety. In a broken system, when even just one agent uses their authority for good, the door to justice begins to open. Shifting Power The very next day, my colleagues at International Justice Mission (IJM) and I were able to bring the girls to safety and long-term holistic aftercare. I continued to visit the girls for years, witnessing their healing as they moved into new lives of freedom. But nearly 25 years after that night in jail, the fight remains the same; we must not leave until those with governing power wield their power to protect the most vulnerable. If we fail to intervene for the women and girls being brutalized by violent criminals, including intimate partners and family members, the alternative is unconscionable. But when we do show up, we get to be part of shifting the levers of power. Entire systems – even the most corrupt and unjust – begin to change for good. In the 21st century, we must reckon with the reality that millions of women and girls are still not any more safe from violence than they have been in any previous era. It is still true, as it has been for decades, that one in three women will experience physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. Today, and in fact, every day, 140 women will be killed by their partners or family members. But far too often, law enforcement and other government actors appear to be on the side of violent perpetrators and other abusers, rather than those who are suffering violence. Whether it’s taking bribes to protect traffickers, criminalizing women and children who are being exploited, or allowing them to be intimidated into not reporting the abuse, agents of the law bear tremendous responsibility and opportunity to change the systemic violence they have enabled to perpetuate. Violent crime thrives on opportunity, and the argument for countering this could not be more clear: strengthening justice systems deters violence. When laws are enforced and traffickers and other abusers are held accountable, other perpetrators of violence are discouraged from committing similar crimes. I think of this as flipping the fear equation. When violent abusers begin to fear the consequences of law, women and children begin to live free from fear. articles.content_zh: 我经常被问及在东南亚监狱度过的夜晚, 但首要问题并不在于我为何入狱。 相反,为什么这三个女孩要入狱? 为什么是他们,而不是那些从家人那里夺走他们,并反复出卖他们的性生活,把他们的生活变成残酷的噩梦的人? 为什么不让那个把录音带放入年轻女孩口中的女人 让强奸她的男人不会被她尖叫所打扰 系统失败了 妓院老板被告知他们的营救行动,允许她隐瞒罪行,并说要把女孩们扔到附近的一个公交站。 本应救出他们的警察却以移民指控逮捕了他们。 贩卖者走得自由,而女孩则被当作罪犯对待. 当晚我和她们坐在一起时,我渴望那些女孩从来没有被关进监狱,更不用说妓院了。 我希望他们总是和家人一起在家,上学,和朋友一起玩. 我希望他们从一开始就没有受到伤害。 但是,现实是,同我们当今世界上数百万妇女和女童一样,她们遭受了司法制度被打破所造成的后果。 所以,我和女孩们在一起的原因 就是另一种选择太可怕了。 我宁愿自己被捕,而不是让他们受到进一步的攻击。 但有一个重要的细节需要澄清:最后,我不需要过夜。 一旦我明白我不会离开, 看守自己承担了保证他们安全的责任。 在一个破碎的体系中,即使只有一个特工善用权威,正义之门也开始打开. 正在移动电源 第二天,我在国际司法特派团(正义团)的同事和我得以使这些女孩安全地得到长期的全面照顾。 多年来,我继续探访这些女孩,目睹她们进入自由新生活时愈合。 但是,在狱中当晚近25年之后,这场战斗依然如故;我们决不能离开,直到那些拥有统治权的人行使权力保护最脆弱群体。 如果我们不能干预暴力罪犯,包括亲密伴侣和家庭成员对妇女和女孩的残暴行为,那么,另一种选择是不合理的。 但是,当我们出现时, 我们就会成为改变权力杠杆的一部分。 整个系统 — — 甚至最腐败和最不公正的系统 — — 开始永远改变。 在21世纪,我们必须考虑这样一个现实:数百万妇女和女童仍然比以往任何时代都更无法免遭暴力。 几十年来,每3个妇女中就有1个在一生中遭受身体或性暴力。 今天,事实上,每天都有140名妇女被其伴侣或家庭成员杀害。 但是,执法部门和其他政府行为者似乎往往站在暴力肇事者和其他施虐者一边,而不是那些遭受暴力的人一边。 无论是收受贿赂来保护被剥削的妇女和儿童,还是让他们受到恐吓来不报告虐待,法律工作者都肩负着巨大的责任和机会来改变他们得以延续的系统性暴力。 暴力犯罪依靠机会而兴起,打击暴力的论据再清楚不过了:加强司法系统可以阻止暴力。 当法律得到实施,贩运者和其他施虐者被追究责任时,其他暴力行为的犯罪人就被劝阻不犯下类似的罪行。 我认为这是在改变恐惧的等式。 当暴力虐待者开始害怕法律的后果时,妇女和儿童开始免于恐惧地生活。 在与IJM的合作中, 我帮助建立了一个模型, 我们非常谨慎

articles.summary_zh: 一名在土耳其东部船形编队工作的雷达科学家说，他的扫描显示里面有组织的图案、腔室和走廊，这些特征不是天然岩石。根据该项目的说法，科学家Khosrow Bakhtar是一位资深的美国国防科学家，也是现场使用的BakhtarRadar系统的发明者。
articles.title_zh: 研究人员说，雷达显示土耳其船形编队内的房间和走廊，有些人认为是诺亚方舟
articles.content: A radar scientist working at a boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey says his scans show organized patterns, chambers and corridors inside it, and that those features are not natural rock. The scientist, Khosrow Bakhtar, is a veteran U.S. defense scientist and the inventor of the BakhtarRadar system used at the site, according to the project’s release. He reported the preliminary results from inside the Durupınar Formation, a roughly 515-foot structure near Mount Ararat that Ark hunters have studied since 1959. Bakhtar said the radar was set to mask natural geological signals, so a purely natural anomaly would not have shown up in the processed images. He called it “the most significant finding of 45 years of my career.” Prof. Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University, who oversees the permitted project, reviewed and confirmed the preliminary results, the release says. He added that the radar also shows a structure with three levels, which he compared to the three levels of the Ark in “our Holy Books.” The findings were presented at a symposium in Turkey, and the group, Noah’s Ark Scans, announced them this week. The group also reports recovering charred wood from almost 30 feet down inside the formation, and says the condition of the wood is what makes it interesting. Genesis describes the Ark coated in pitch, which burns easily, so the release suggests someone may have tried to set the Ark on fire long ago. Charring slows decomposition in soil, often to well under 1% a year, so “what was meant to destroy it may have actually preserved it,” the release says. The group also says the wood is not recent surface debris and was not carried in by mudflow, because it came from deep within the formation. The release allows other explanations for the charring, including lightning or volcanic activity. Founder Andrew Jones said the wood could be the charred remains of the Ark or the remains of a campfire a shepherd lit while using it for shelter centuries ago. The wood has been sent for carbon-14 dating and species identification, and the team says no firm conclusions should be drawn until the results are published. Dating would give the wood’s age and identification would show what kind of tree it came from, but neither result would by itself show that it came from a boat. Everything here comes from the group itself. The radar results are preliminary, the masking is the team’s own processing, and none of it has been through independent peer review. A 1996 study by geologist Lorence Collins and Ark hunter David Fasold concluded that Durupınar is a natural rock formation. Noah’s Ark Scans also sells guided tours and merchandise, is running a GiveSendGo fundraiser for more core drilling, and its release asks for donations and points readers to a gold dealer and a preparedness retailer. More radar processing and reporting is expected in the coming months, and Jones has said initial lab results are expected over the winter. Atila has said photos of the wood will be released in the near future.
articles.content_zh: 一位在土耳其东部的船形编队工作的雷达科学家说,他的扫描显示它内部有条理的图案,室室和走廊,这些特征不是天然岩石. 科学家Khosrow Bakhtar是一位美国资深国防科学家, 他报告了Durupınar Formation公司内部的初步结果,这是Ararat山附近一个约515英尺高的结构,由Ark猎人自1959年以来研究。 巴赫塔尔说,雷达是用来遮掩自然地质信号的,因此在经过处理的图像中不会出现纯粹的自然异常. 他称之为“我45年职业生涯中最重要的发现”。 师曰. Sivas Cumhuriyet大学的Cenker Atila监督了许可的项目,审查并确认了初步结果。 他补充说,雷达还显示一个具有三个级别的结构,他与方舟子在“我们的圣书”中的三个级别相比。 调查结论在土耳其的一次研讨会上发表, 剧组还报告从形成地近30英尺下方取出烧焦的木头,并说木头的状况使得它很有趣. "创世记"描述了被涂入花筒的"方舟",这很容易被烧伤,因此发行表明有人可能早就想放出"方舟"了. 碳化物在土壤中的分解速度慢了,每年的分解率往往不到1%,因此“破坏它的意图可能是实际保存下来的”。 剧组还称该木不是近代地表出土出土的地表出土出土后被泥流所承载,因为它出土出土了形成地深. 释放后可以对焦炭进行其他解释,包括闪电或火山活性. 创始人安德鲁·琼斯(Andrew Jones)说,木头可能是"方舟"被烧焦的遗骨,也可能是数百年前在使用时被牧羊人点燃了的营火的遗骨. 该木被送去进行碳-14约会和物种鉴定,队伍表示在结果公布之前不应得出确定的结论. 约会可以说明木材的年代, 这里的一切来自团体本身. 雷达结果初步,口罩是团队自己的处理方式,没有经过独立的同行评审. 1996年由地质学家洛伦斯·柯林斯和方克猎人大卫·法拉尔德进行的一项研究得出结论,杜鲁普纳尔是天然岩层. 诺亚方舟扫描公司也出售导游和商品, 预计未来几个月会有更多的雷达处理和报告,琼斯表示预计冬季会有初步的实验室结果. Atila表示, 木头的照片将在不久的将来发布。

articles.title_zh: 盖洛普： 30岁以下美国人的生活水平比2010年低20个百分点
articles.content: A 25-year-old in 2026 is starting adult life in worse shape than a 25-year-old in 2010, at least by their own account. Gallup’s newest wellbeing report finds that 44% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 29 are “thriving” so far this year, down from a high of 64% in 2010. Gallup counts someone as thriving if they rate their current life a 7 or higher on a zero-to-10 ladder and expect to rate their life an 8 or higher five years from now. Most of the drop came recently. About two-thirds of the total decline has happened since 2019. Gallup is careful about causes, saying a set of factors “may explain” the decline among young adults. It points to a rise in depression, weaker close relationships, less daily enjoyment and less feeling active and productive each day. It also lists lower satisfaction with living standards, with leaders who create enthusiasm about the future and with progress toward personal goals. Among adults 30 to 44, it says the share currently having or being treated for depression is up 15 points since 2019, to 37%. Beyond those measures, Gallup names loneliness, which it says has been particularly acute among younger men, along with housing affordability and fear of losing jobs to AI. About half of adults 18 to 49 doubt Medicare and Social Security will be available in 10 years, far more than other age groups. Just 14% of adults 18 to 34 say they are “extremely proud” to be American, down 10 points since 2025. The numbers follow people as they age. Adults now 34 to 46 are at 46%, compared with 64% when they were the 18-to-29 group in 2010, so their ratings fell as they got older while the young adults behind them are starting from a lower place. Adults 30 to 44 are at 45%, down from a high of 62% in 2016 and 2017. Adults 45 to 64 are at 46%, which matches their low from 2008. The estimates come from three Gallup Panel surveys in February, May and August 2026 with 15,156 U.S. adults in total.

articles.content: Franni Cash was about 13 when she says the community her family belonged to officially became a cult. She was 17 when her family left it. She told RELEVANT that her parents joined after their marriage hit a rough patch and a friend suggested counseling. The therapist they saw, she said, was “dangerously smart” and used people’s vulnerabilities “to kind of tether loyalty to himself.” Counseling sessions became Bible studies with other families, and then she says they were told they no longer needed church. Eventually the leader declared himself their spiritual father and warned that anyone who broke covenant with him would be cut off, and women who disagreed with their husbands were said to have “the Jezebel spirit.” “It just became so far away from the truth,” Cash said. She kept a diary about how strange it all felt. The leader found it and burned it. She was 14. “From that place I pushed it down,” she said. “I can’t question it and can’t voice this anymore.” Her family left in the middle of her senior year of high school, after an article exposed years of alleged fraud and sexual allegations tied to the leader. She remembers her parents telling the kids in their bedroom. “It was like this weight flew off my shoulders,” she said. Then came a harder year, when she feared the curses and watched her brothers struggle. “I didn’t know if I was gonna make it. I really mean that.” Her parents put the family in therapy immediately. Talk therapy alone didn’t work for her, because she was still so brainwashed she didn’t know what she could say. EMDR and brainspotting did. She has been in consistent therapy for ten years now and says talking about the cult no longer stings. “I’ve had to grieve them being susceptible to something so harmful,” she said of her parents. “But right off the bat, they got themselves in therapy.” She describes her healing journey as medicine and scripture working together. “You can’t just slap a Bible verse on it,” she said. “Scripture is so powerful, but sometimes you don’t know how to absorb it until you can do some surgery.” The family’s first song came a year and a half after they left, and it became We the Kingdom. Cash said the band was a place where she felt understood, because her family were the only people who could laugh at the jokes instead of being horrified. She also says they were trauma bonded, and that she needed to learn who she was on her own. She left the band, and says she and her family are now the closest they’ve ever been, “from a health and respect” place that “doesn’t feel enmeshed.” Her solo debut, Here I Am , takes its title from a lyric she and her father, producer and songwriter Ed Cash, wrote together for the song “The Real Thing”: Here I am, I made it through. The page is burned, but this story is not over. Here I Am was also going to be the title of an album she planned at 16, in the middle of everything. “Now here I am, kind of on the other side of healing,” she said. Getting there meant relearning music. A friend, the writer Paul Duncan, told her she needed to “date music like you would your spouse,” meaning listen to records she loved as a kid with no goal. She was driving on the Pacific Coast Highway when U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name” came on. “It was like I heard music for the first time,” she said. She has since been listening to Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On , Al Green, Elton John, Casey Musgraves, John Mayer and Linkin Park’s Hybrid Theory . Her view of God changed too. “I just really thought that God was this angry man upstairs,” she said. She remembers being told to get off the worship stool because she wasn’t “anointed enough.” Then she met what she calls the real Jesus. “He was so loving. And gracious with me,” she said. “It changed everything.” When we asked what she’d say to someone inside a controlling church, her answer was short. “Leave. You’re free to. articles.content: The search bar in a Bible app works like any other, which means it shows what people are worried about before they’ve said it out loud to anyone. YouVersion says “Psalm 91” was the single most-searched term in the app this year. In its newest release , the company also says “anxiety,” “hope” and “healing” were among the year’s most searched terms. YouVersion describes Psalm 91 as a psalm that encourages readers to turn to God for refuge and comfort in difficult times. The psalm runs 16 verses. Together, YouVersion says, the searches offer a glimpse into the personal questions and hopes people are bringing to Scripture. Daily use of the Bible App grew by more than 13% compared with 2025, reaching 18.5 million people a day. It also says it added more than 160 million new installs across its family of apps in 2026, after celebrating one billion installs last November. Daily engagement grew faster than installs, which the company reads as a sign that people are returning to the app and not only downloading it. Some of the highest engagement is outside the U.S. YouVersion says it sees some of the highest levels of Bible App engagement in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and it is building regional hubs in places including the United Kingdom, Brazil, Kenya and Mexico. Its apps offer 3,800 versions of the Bible in 2,400 languages, and it works with a network of more than 45,000 churches and partners. Bobby Gruenewald, YouVersion’s founder and CEO, said in the release that the company has been encouraged by “how many people are turning to Scripture for answers to their questions.”

articles.summary: Widow's Bay  and the Trolley Problem of Life   The post  Fear Itself  appeared first on  Mockingbird .

articles.title_zh: 恐惧自身
articles.content: W hat is your biggest fear? Spiders? That’s a classic. Deranged clowns? Sure! Maybe you prefer the more existential variety? How about never fully realizing your potential or dying alone? All of the above? Similar to the What superpower would you choose? question, it is hard for me to select only one. I am a fearful person. I have a way of collecting fears as I go about my life. Alpha-gal, something I did not know existed until two days ago, is the flavor of the week. But my fear of dying alone is more like a longtime, trusted companion. The world is a scary place. At any moment, our identities could be hacked. Our phones could ring with dreadful news. Our brains could suffer an aneurysm. Swimming in a bottomless sea of insecurity, we are meagerly equipped with our basic survival instincts: fight, flight, freeze, and appease. These impulses may help keep us safe from spiders and clowns (answer for both: flight!), but what do we make of the dangers that are harder to pin down? What if the dangers are not only without but within? Leave it to this year’s hit TV series to explore these questions. If you’re looking for a spooky show to get into this weekend, it’s Widow’s Bay. The Emmy-sweeping, genre-bending, horror-comedic series is a triumph for a number of reasons. For starters, it muddles the black-and-white worlds Hollywood has created (e.g., horror movies without humor, comedies without any depth), reminding us that life can be both scary and funny. The show has all the irresistible horror tropes (the harbinger who warns everyone of impending doom, the suspenseful music, the jump scares) but, along with its crowd-pleasing antics, it dives deeper than surface-level fears. Its anthropology is refreshingly low. This is not a match between good people and evil monsters. Yes, sometimes the enemy is a chainsaw-wielding fiend. Much scarier, however, is when the enemy is yourself. Take Tom Loftis, for instance, the ambitious new mayor who wants to transform the cursed island town of Widow’s Bay into the next Martha’s Vineyard. He is, from every angle, a secular man. For Tom, God is no more real than ghosts. The only higher power that exists is the one you achieve by climbing the ladder. He resents how the locals tolerate the town’s haunted reputation. For too long, people have been resigned to the rumors that the hotel is haunted, the church is cursed, and the bay isn’t safe for a swim. For Tom, the only thing to fear is fear itself. Like any mayor with a messiah complex, he sets out to do something about it. As Loftis sees things, the real problem with the place is not that it is demonically possessed. The real problem is bad branding . In his eyes, Widow’s Bay is simply misunderstood. When visiting Widow’s Bay to write a piece for the New York Times travel section, a reporter asks Loftis about a framed article in the historical society titled “Cannibalism in God’s House.” Loftis tries to water it down. “These stories get so exaggerated over time,” he says. “Was there a deadly storm in 1786? Yes. Did a group of people get trapped inside a church? Apparently so. Did they immediately turn to cannibalism? No, that took four days !” See? That’s not so bad, right? Loftis’ PR campaign is like slapping new siding on a haunted mansion. He is convinced that the plight of Widow’s Bay can be solved by installing a proper cappuccino machine in the local coffee shop. Cappuccino machines are great at making a proper latte but pretty useless when up against the occult. Before long, Loftis’ denial of the curse over the island town is just as dangerous as the curse itself. The first step to keeping the forces at bay is to admit they exist. There is a scene in which Loftis speaks to another character about the Trolley Problem, an ethical thought experiment in which there is a runaway trolley barreling down the tracks toward a crowd of people. articles.content_zh: 帽子是你最大的恐惧? 蜘蛛吗? 这是经典。 疯狂的小丑? 当然! 也许你更喜欢生存的品种? 永远不能充分发挥你的潜力 或孤独地死去怎么样? 所有这一切? 类似于你选择的超级大国? 问,我很难只选一个 我是一个害怕的人。 我有办法收集恐惧 当我去我的生活。 Alpha -gal,我两天前才知道的东西 是这个星期的口味 但我害怕孤独地死去 更像是长期 值得信赖的同伴 世界是个可怕的地方。 我们的身份随时可能被黑入 我们的电话可能会传出可怕的消息 我们的大脑可能会有动脉瘤 在一个不安全的无底海中游来游去,我们装备了我们的基本生存本能:战斗、出逃、冻结和安抚。 这些冲动也许可以帮助我们远离蜘蛛和小丑(回答:飞行!),但我们如何应对那些更难消除的危险? 如果危险不仅是没有危险,而且是内部危险呢? 让今年的电视连续剧来探讨这些问题。 如果你想要一个恐怖的节目进入这个周末, "艾美扫地"(英語:Emmy-sweating, genre-bending),"恐怖喜剧"(英語:Description-comed)系列,由于多种原因,是一场胜利. 首先,它搅乱了好莱坞所创造的黑白世界(例如没有幽默感的恐怖电影,没有任何深度的喜剧),提醒我们生活既会恐怖又会搞笑. 该节目拥有所有不可抗拒的恐怖颤抖(预告会警告所有人即将来临的末日,悬疑的音乐,跳跃的惊吓等),但连同其人群取悦的焦虑,其潜入比地表恐惧更深. 它的人类学水平低得惊人 这不是好人和邪恶怪物的对决 是的,有时敌人是一个 链锯的恶魔。 然而,更可怕的是当敌人是你自己的时候。 以汤姆·洛夫蒂斯(Tom Loftis)为例, 他,从每个角度来说,都是世俗的人. 对汤姆来说,上帝不比鬼更真实. 唯一高的电能是通过攀登梯子实现的. 当地民众如何容忍镇上闹事的名声? 久而久之,人们对旅馆闹鬼、教堂被诅咒、海湾游泳不安全等谣言辞职。 对汤姆来说,唯一害怕的是恐惧本身. 像任何拥有救世主建筑群的市长一样,他开始对此有所行动. 正如洛夫提斯所见 这个地方真正的问题不是 它被恶魔附身 真正的问题是品牌不好 在他眼中,寡妇湾只是被误解了。 当一位记者访问寡妇湾为纽约时报旅行部写出一篇作品时,他问洛夫蒂斯关于历史社会中一篇被设定为“神殿中的食人狂”的文章。 洛夫提斯试图给它浇水 他说,“这些故事随着时间的推移变得如此夸张。” “1786年是否有致命的风暴? 对 一群人被困在教堂里了吗? 显然如此。 他们有没有立即转向吃人? 不,那需要四天时间!” 这还不算太糟吧? Loftis的公关活动就像在闹鬼的豪宅上再拍一拍。 他相信寡妇湾的困境可以通过在当地咖啡店安装适当的卡布奇诺机器来解决。 卡布奇诺机器很擅长做一个正宗的拿铁 但和神秘主义作对时却很没用 不久之后,洛夫蒂斯否认对岛屿城镇的诅咒,与诅咒本身同样危险。 阻止势力存在的第一步是承认它们的存在. 有个场景让洛夫蒂斯向另一个角色讲述了"特罗莱问题"(Trolley Problem),这是一场道德思想实验,其中有一个跑跑的推车管向一行人冲去. 在这个假想的设定中,有一个杠杆,可以把推车换到只有一跑道的另一跑道.

articles.content: No matter who won or lost the last big game you attended, chances are, Ozzy Osbourne was there in electronic chains, locked inside a brain-rattling sound system, unnoticed, unnamed, misunderstood, a voice crying in the wilderness of crowded rows of fans desperate for a win, cheering for their heroes while jeering at their opponents, paying too much for unnecessary carbs and calories, possibly on the sabbath day. When Ozzy cried, “All aboard!” you stood with hundreds or thousands of tangential warriors singing along with the fatalistic chorus, air guitaring with the riffs, nodding with the rhythm, but you weren’t there for music. You were there to shout, thump your chest, flex, thrust hands with fingers contorted into symbols of specific allegiance, or claim you’re #1, convinced that the song, the battle cry, and the power behind it all were on your side. The words didn’t matter. Your heroes were fighting for you, to give you hope. You’d fight for them if you could, if you had to, against whoever stands in your way, to win at all costs. But what if that’s not what Ozzy wanted? How do we know what he wanted? He screams, “You’ve got to listen to my words!” Below is a paraphrase of the “Crazy Train” lyrics: “It’s crazy, but it’s always been like this — we’re all living as enemies. But maybe it’s not too late to learn how to love and forget how to hate. We’ve all got mental wounds that aren’t healing. I’m losing it. I’ve listened to everyone — fools, preachers, anarchists. Nothing helps. There’s always a system run by someone who’s a product of the system and has been conditioned to run the system, which is sold to us by rich people who get richer by keeping the system alive. And we buy it, screaming in pain from our open mental wounds. It’s messed up. I’m messed up. We’re all messed up. We inherit each other’s trouble. We’re heirs of unresolved conflict. I keep saying it, but no one listens. You’ve got to listen to my words. I can’t figure out how to feel. The mental wounds don’t heal. I don’t know who to blame, but I know it’s not fair.” I wrote the above paraphrase to read to my senior literature class last Monday morning. Nearly half of the students in the class are varsity football starters chasing championships and full-rides. I prefaced the reading with a white lie, “I got this message from someone you all know over the weekend. I won’t tell you who it is, but I want you to help me think through how to respond.” The starting quarterback, worried, tried to interrupt me. I didn’t look up, held my hand out to pause questions, and continued reading. When I finished, there was a chorus of concern from several voices: That’s a cry for help! Is it from a boy or a girl? You said we know them? Who is it? Did they email you? What did you say? They need help. Who are you going to talk to? Still in character, I said, “I can’t tell you a name, but I’ll play this song.” A few seconds into “Crazy Train,” the students realized what was going on, looked relieved, but then became uncomfortable when I turned down the volume and read out the actual lyrics. In confused silence, their faces said, We weren’t listening . I felt bad. I smiled and apologized for manipulating their emotions, and the air lightened. Someone started singing the chorus, and we moved on. But I’m not sure we should have. “Crazy Train” is the most popular song from the most recognizable sex, drugs, and rock-n-roll villain to ever bite the head off a bat, but it’s also a cry for help from a struggling human admitting personal weakness and claiming no superiority. While suggesting that love is better than hate, he’s doing more than just asking us to love. He’s asking us to LEARN HOW TO. French philosopher and mystic, Simone Weil, who died during World War II in solidarity with residents of German-occupied France, didn’t write how-to books, but she couldn’t stop talking about attention. articles.title_zh: East Coker和治疗人类残疾的方法
articles.content: H ow strange that one can read the same poems countless times and discover new things with each visit, like a traveler coming home for Christmas only to find it slightly altered! It is the same for me revisiting T. S. Eliot’s Four Quartets : the end is different than I imagined in the beginning when I first read these words, imagined these places, and attempted to grasp the author’s meaning. Eliot had the same experience. The meaning of the Four Quartets was one thing when he originally envisioned them, another when he wrote them, and still another when the public began analyzing them. He never believed they would be forever linked with the world’s most destructive war. He had not even known there would be four. In the beginning, there was only “Burnt Norton,” written in 1936 and intended to be a one-off. It was generally well received by critics, and the whole business could have been over then. But three years passed, and Eliot found himself with that most common of authorly ailments: not knowing what to write or fearing that he no longer knew how to write properly. Specifically, he had gone for some time without constructing new poems. The world had changed since “Burnt Norton” was published. A growing menace once possible to ignore had exploded into a firestorm of destructive force sweeping through the nations of Europe, consuming all in its path. The bonds that had knit together what remained of Western Christian civilization were snapping with wild abandon, supplanted by ideologies of extermination. Faced with such a crisis, Eliot searched for the one fixed point amid the whirling chaos. He settled on the village of East Coker in Somerset, England. His ancestor Andrew Eliot had left there in 1669, abandoning the historic family home and immigrating to New England. Nearly three centuries later, Thomas Stearns Eliot had become the first member of the family to move back to the motherland, and the family connection held spiritual significance for him. In 1937, he visited St. Michael and All Angels’ Church in East Coker, where his ashes would one day be placed. I know something of Eliot’s experience. I too am the descendant of Englishmen and women whose bones lie buried in every corner of that land, some in tombs I have visited. I too was the first person in my family to return and live in England, if only for a year. It did feel in a sense like returning to my beginning, which is probably why I connect so strongly with the Four Quartets . The secret Eliot discovered at East Coker is one that has transformed my own life as well: we do not possess the power to redeem ourselves or the world and are utterly dependent on the gift of grace. Of all the Four Quartets , this is the most law and gospel poem. The Four Quartets are commonly associated with the four traditional elements of the physical world: air, earth, water, and fire. But as I have noted, Eliot did not begin with a grand plan, so the elemental symbolism becomes stronger in the later poems. Yes, we see the movement of air in “Burnt Norton” disturbing a bowl of rose leaves and carrying the laughter of children, but you would not conclude “This is an air poem” unless you had the other three Quartets to guide you. Likewise, the earth theme is not obvious after the first section of “East Coker,” but once we get to “The Dry Salvages,” we will be drowned in water imagery, and “Little Gidding” will pelt us with fire from beginning to end. Thus, Eliot begins “East Coker” rooted in the earth, in time and place and home. But immediately, the earth is overturned by the machinations of human societies succeeding and supplanting one another, building up to heaven and returning to dust. In my beginning is my end. In succession Houses rise and fall, crumble, are extended, Are removed, destroyed, restored, or in their place Is an open field, or a factory, or a by-pass. articles.content_zh: 奇怪的是,人们可以阅读同名诗作无数次,每次拜访都会发现新的事物,就像一个旅行者回家过圣诞节,只为了发现它略有改变! 我同样重温了T. S. Eliot的四重奏:结局和我最初读到这些话、想象这些地方并试图理解作者含义时所想象的不一样。 Eliot也有同样的经历. 四重奏的意义是他最初设想它们的时候是一回事,他写它们的时候是另一回事,当公众开始分析它们的时候仍然是另一回事. 他从未相信它们会永远与世界上最具破坏性的战争联系在一起。 他甚至不知道会有四个。 一开始只有"伯恩特·诺顿"(Burnt Norton,作于1936年)一作一作一作一想. 它普遍受到批评者的好评,整个业务本来可以到那时结束. 但三年过去了,艾略特发现自己与最常见的作者病症相伴:不知道该写什么,或担心自己不再知道如何正确写作. 具体地说,他已经走了一段时间,没有创作出新诗. 自“Burnt Norton”出版以来,世界发生了变化。 日益严重的威胁一旦可能被忽视,就已演变成一股由毁灭性力量横扫欧洲各国并吞噬其道路的火焰。 将西方基督教文明遗留下来的东西联系起来的纽带,被被灭绝思想所取代而疯狂地抛弃了。 面对这样的危机,埃利奥特在旋转的混乱中寻找一个固定点. 他定居于英格兰萨默塞特的东科克村. 他的祖先安德鲁·埃利奥特于1669年离开那里,放弃了有历史意义的家族家园并移民到新英格兰. 近3个世纪后,托马斯·斯蒂恩斯·埃利奥特成为了第一个搬回祖国的家庭成员,家庭联系对他具有了精神意义. 1937年,他参观了东科克的圣迈克尔和All Angels教堂,在那里有一天他的骨灰会被放置. 我知道Eliot的经验。 我也是英国男人和女人的后人 他们的骨头埋在这片土地的每一个角落, 一些在我的访问过的坟墓。 我也是我家里第一个回到英国生活的人 哪怕只有一年 我确实感觉回到我的开始, 这可能是为什么我如此紧密地与四重奏联系起来。 Eliot在东科克发现的秘密 也改变了我自己的生活: 我们没有拯救自己或世界的能力, 完全依赖恩赐。 在所有四重奏中,这是最有法律和福音的诗. 四重奏通常与物理世界的四大传统元素相通:空气,地,水,火. 但正如我所指出,艾略特并没有从一个宏伟的计划入手,因此元素符号主义在后期诗作中变得更加强大. 是的,我们看到“Burnt Norton”中的空气运动扰乱了一碗玫瑰叶并带了孩子们的笑声,但除非有另外三个四方来指导你,否则你不会得出“这是一首空气诗”的结论。 同样地,在第一部分“东科克”之后,地球主题并不明显,但一旦我们到达“干涸的盐水”,我们将被水上图像所淹没,而“小吉丁”将从头到尾向我们开火。 因此,Eliot开始“东科克”扎根于地球、时间、地点和家园。 但是,立即,人类社会的成功和取而代之的诡计推翻了地球,使地球升入天堂并回到了尘土中。 在我开始的时候,就是我的结局。 房屋的起伏、倒塌、被延长、被拆除、被摧毁、被恢复或取代,都是空地、工厂或旁道。 如果你曾参观过萨利斯伯里平原上古老的巨石阵纪念碑 你知道它坐落在一条相交的公路上

articles.content: Listeners will have a better idea of why The Mockingcast works (or doesn’t) and why they keep tuning in, 11 years later. We included a few such stories at the beginning of the 300 th episode , and the tears I shed were real. But I thought take the opportunity to offer a few observations from behind the curtain about what I personally appreciate about our podcast, what I’m most proud of, and what’s been challenging. No doubt my co-hosts would have other aspects they’d highlight. First, the longevity. It’s worth celebrating, even if it’s both a blessing and a curse. The time has allowed us to develop some pretty priceless chemistry. When I’m picking articles for us to talk about, I know that even if the material falls flat, I can rely on our dynamic to take up the slack. I trust my co-hosts, and it’s been very gratifying to watch us gel in a non-contrived way over the years. We’ve been through a lot together, and it shows, I think. Being around so long (in internet years) means we’ve had the benefit of watching things come and go. Sarah mentioned this recently in relation to the moralization of food in our society. It was super acute about eight years ago, then it retreated a bit with the body-positivity moment, now it’s back again under the guise of #maxxing. But that’s just one example. I could mention radical atheism, or gospel-centered this and that, or mindfulness. We’ve seen cultural fixations take hold and then recede, specific anxieties bubble up and dissipate. The longer view allows for a measure of perspective that I believe lends the show added depth. Longevity can also be a curse. The ebb and flow can foster a degree of detachment that masquerades as superiority. For example, it’s hard to take the latest rebranding of medieval monasticism (or justification by works) seriously when you’ve seen it happen four times under four different (best-selling) names already. Discipline becomes application becomes virtue becomes formation and so on. It’s a challenge to keep listening and paying attention, but a challenge that I’m proud of us for at least trying to live up to. Because beneath every one of the trends we’ve observed are real people with real hopes and dreams and disappointments. The second longevity-related challenge is the same one that afflicts anyone in a public role, especially those in ministry or thought life. It’s the danger of impersonating yourself. Whenever I detect in my voice any sense of “the grace guy needs to say a grace thing now” — it makes my skin crawl. Autopilot is the enemy, along with its cousin repetition. I remember a trusted listener once warning me that we were becoming a podcast about social media. Another said we were talking too much about parenting. These grooves are understandable, but to keep things fresh, especially over the long haul, you have to always be finding fresh vistas, not just in the culture but in yourself. It’s not easy. This leads me to the next observation: over ten years, it’s become notably more difficult to find suitable material for The Mockingcast . One of the things that I hold sacred about our show is its role as a refuge from culture wars. I want listeners to be confident that when they press play, we’re not going to trigger them about the same headlines that trigger them the rest of the day. We haven’t done this perfectly, I realize, but it remains a guiding principle. When the occasional how-dare-you emails come in, folks are usually surprised to hear that they come just as frequently from both sides of the aisle. If they didn’t, I’d try to course correct. Finding stuff that threads the needle of interesting and substantial but not pre-narrativized has gotten more challenging over our tenure. It’s like the ledge we walk has gotten narrower. Not nonexistent, mind you, just narrower. I’m so proud we’ve reached this milestone without, at least in my view, falling into an ideological ditch or becoming (too) predictable. articles.title_zh: 恩典的谣言
articles.content: “You only work on Sundays, anyway.” One of the go-to jokes of a group of guys I hang out with. I laugh because, well, I just like to please people. But every time the boys say it, I think to myself, “If you only knew what being a pastor feels like sometimes.” An impromptu funeral at the clinic for veterinarians whose colleague committed suicide, scrolling to find an angry email about last week’s sermon or the changing of the carpet color in the narthex, begging financial generosity from people who pay your salary, lunch with a lonely man going through a brutal divorce, restocking the youth fridge with 7,000 Cheerwines, hearing that they’re gossiping about you again, failing yet again to prepare a sermon that marries TikTok and TED Talk, off to the shelter to serve dinner, did I even eat lunch? Did I mention that this was last Tuesday? Ministry is often pure gift. The highs are as high as they get. Pastors bear witness to the most intimate, most raw, most human, most beautiful and terrifying moments of people’s lives. We play at the level of the soul. We get paid to read and write and pray. We have a front-row seat to miracles: the bound freed, the sinner forgiven, the debts paid, the dead resurrected. It’s not lost on me that having a job rife with meaning is a privilege and honor. This is what God has chosen to make of my life, and I am truly grateful. And yet, there’s no way to get away from the fact that ministry is a burden too. Its shape is a cross. Its form is death and resurrection. People bring all their junk to church — and they should. Sunday mornings are not an assembly of the righteous, they are a sanctuary for sinners — hypocrites anonymous, I like to call it. articles.content: 1. “ ‘I Shall Be Very Surprised If There Isn’t A Next Chapter’ ” is the title of the remarkable interview with English theologian Sarah Coakley that appeared on the New York Times website this past week, courtesy of Peter Wehner. We’ve been at this Another Week Ends game for a couple decades now, and I’m not sure I’ve ever seen so much theological substance published in America’s once-and-future(?) paper of record. I’ve been aware of Coakley’s work and reputation for some time but never taken the plunge, which, after reading their conversation, feels like a bit of a shame-on-me situation. One of my favorite bits comes at the very beginning, when Coakley talks about her teenage years. Apparently the confirmation classes at her little Church of England parish lacked the rigor she was hoping for. Thus, she did what all kids that age do these days: My eldest brother and I organized our own theological discussion group in that same parish. We brought a lot of our atheistical and skeptical school friends into it. And this very holy rector was very clever at this point, because he just sat watching the arguments go backward and forward, rather like the umpire at Wimbledon. He never intervened, never put us right, never told us what the right answer was. When my brother and I recently thought about who had attended those discussions, the vast majority of our friends who attended at that age, 14 to 16, subsequently became Christians. So that tells you something about opening the Pandora’s box theologically and how important it is for the clergy not to stifle that. A lovely little testament to the power of grace in practice, I’d say, and one which jibes with my own decades working with young people. Allow students to ask their questions, raise their objections and air their doubts without threat of defensiveness — let that stuff hang in the air — and the craziest things can happen, especially over the long haul. Squash their arguments with doctrine, even right doctrine, and you risk alienating them forever. Such is the emotional wallop of correction, however well intentioned. Coakley goes on to provide some rather damning commentary on the gap in theology between the academy and the pew, the professor and the layperson. One of the core hopes of her own work, she claims, is the closing of that gap chasm, to which I can only add a hearty amen. I’ve tried to do something similar in my own books, albeit on a much smaller scale. (Whether utilizing a French phrase for that project — théologie totale — screams accessibility is a separate question.) In Coakley’s view, uncoupling the study of theology from the practice of prayer is dangerous. This leads her into one of the most beautiful articulations of prayer I’ve read anywhere, let alone the New York Times : How do I pray? Well, you hand yourself over to the source of your being, and then you ask some things. But the handing over is primary, and learning how to do that. It changes your perspective on God — because when you practice this, even for a very short time each day, simple opening up space in which God is God. You don’t control it. That’s what’s so frightening. This is not a new skill, like learning how to make a very good omelet or to ride a bicycle. This is a nonskill. It’s an unskilling, an unmastery. It completely changes your view of God, because up to that point you’ve probably subliminally been thinking about God as a very large entity, the largest and the best in a universe of entities whom somehow you’ve got to get on your side or cajole or get to answer your request. I know that’s a very naïve sounding description, but as a priest I can tell you that’s the God I hear about all the time. All the great theologians of the tradition have slain that God, and they’ve had to slay that God — think of Luther — with great terror. It’s really just opening up to the possibility of grace. articles.content_zh: 1. " `I Shall Be very Surprise If There Isout A Next Chapter ' ”是英国神学家Sarah Coakley在上周在纽约时报网站上发表的令人瞩目的访谈的标题,由Peter Wehner主持。 我不确定我是否曾见过如此多的神学物质, 我了解Coakley的作品与名声已有一段时间, 我最喜欢的一点 是在一开始, 当Coakley谈论她的青少年时代。 显然,她的英格兰小教堂的确认课 缺乏她希望的严格度。 因此,她做了所有的孩子 这些天做: 我的长兄和我在同一堂区组织了我们自己的神学讨论小组。 我们把许多无神论和怀疑论的学校朋友都带进了其中. 而这位非常神圣的校长 此时非常聪明, 因为他只是坐着看着这些争论往后走, 就像温布尔登的裁判。 他从来没有干预,从来没有让我们正确,从来没有告诉我们什么是正确的答案。 当我和我兄弟最近想到谁参加了这些讨论时,14至16岁的我们绝大多数朋友后来成为基督徒。 因此,这可以说明在神学上打开潘多拉的盒子,以及神职人员不要扼杀它的重要性。 一个可爱的小证明, 在实践中, 允许学生提问,提出反对意见并表达他们的疑虑,而不会受到防卫威胁——让这些东西被挂在空中——最疯狂的事情可能会发生,特别是在漫长的时间内. 用学说,甚至正确的学说来压制他们的论点,你冒着永远疏远他们的危险. 这是一种精神上的纠错,无论用意如何。 Coakley继续就学院与皮尤,教授和外行人之间的神学差距提供一些相当可憎的评论. 她声称,她自己工作的一个核心希望是,缩小了这一差距,我只能为这一差距增添一个心地阿门。 尽管规模要小得多, (该项目是否使用法语短语-总词-尖叫无障碍是一个单独的问题。 ) 科克利认为,将神学研究与祈祷实践脱钩是危险的. 更别说纽约时报:我该如何祈祷? 你把自己交给你生命的来源 然后问些问题 但交接是初级的, 并学习如何做到这一点。 它改变了你对上帝的看法——因为当你练习这个时,即使每天非常短的时间,简单的打开了上帝是上帝的空间. 你无法控制它。 这才是最可怕的。 这不是一种新的技能,比如学习如何做一个非常好的煎蛋卷或者骑自行车。 这是非技能。 是个没有技能, 这完全改变了你对上帝的看法,因为直到那个时候,你可能一直在深思上帝是一个非常大的实体,是一个最大和最好的实体,你不得不站在你一边,或者说去回答你的要求。 我知道这听起来很天真, 但作为一个牧师,我可以告诉你,这就是我一直听到的上帝。 传统中所有伟大的神学家都杀死了上帝, 他们不得不用巨大的恐怖来杀死上帝—— 想到路德。 这其实只是打开了宽宏大量的可能性。 考虑并不特殊。 这对受过相对教育的人来说非常困难。

articles.content: Welcome back, fiends! Blaine Grimes, Blake Collier, Caleb Stallings, and I are back with the Spooky Season film roundtable, and this week we are watching John Carpenter’s In the Mouth of Madness , the third of his “Apocalypse” films. So file in to Row D, your seat’s a few down from ours and right next to Sam Neill, who’s gulping down popcorn and drawing more crosses on his face. Let’s go a little crazy! Ian : Caleb, what led you to pick In the Mouth of Madness ? Caleb : I actually watched it earlier this year on my quest to see every John Carpenter film. This was the final movie of his I hadn’t seen. And it was the perfect one to end on. An autumnal, meta movie about authorship and terror. Just right up my alley. And what better way to go insane than in an impossibly dark cathedral in an autumnal New England town? Who wouldn’t want to watch a movie about that? And who wouldn’t want it to happen to them too? Ian : Well, when you put it that way … Blake : I was really struck this time by Trent and Cane’s dialogue when Cane states, “I am God now …” and Trent responds something to the effect of “I didn’t know God was a hack horror writer.” It’s a great comeback but also chilling in that humans, no matter their brilliance and no matter how well-adjusted they present as being, are hacks when it comes to authoring their own stories, let alone the stories of others. Only God can weave the narrative in such a way that the goodness, justice, and mercy of the ending is earned. Caleb : And that sanity is maintained! Blake : Exactly! Caleb : If fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, then trying to usurp him is entering the Mouth of Madness. Ian : It is, but it’s a sanity that might look insane to the surrounding world. And that’s the question with Trent, isn’t it? He sounds insane, but he sees through the bogus story Cane is weaving. Blake : In this way, I think the film makes for a thrilling blueprint of the failures of humans trying to weave together the grand narrative of existence, and how fiction can portray our own failures to usurp God’s position and role. Caleb : This reminded me of Tim Keller recounting how Dorothy Sayers wrote herself into her own detective novels to be a help and savior of a sort to her own protagonist, Peter Wimsey. In the Mouth of Madness tells the opposite story: Sutter Cane writes himself into his stories to destroy his characters. Blake : So in this way, Cane is a type of Satan … which means Dante’s footprint is all over this film as well. Blaine : *In Gordon Ramsey voice* Bloody hell. Here we go again … Ian : You know, I’m something of a Dante adaptation myself! We are all creatures spoken into existence, in a story in which, like Sayers, the Teller, the Creator, becomes a character. I think Carpenter was playing with how many people are only familiar with these stories via the film medium, which I imagine is even more true now, 30 years later. And the movie ends, not with Trent rereading Cane’s book to find out how it all ends but rather alone in a theater, eating popcorn and laughing hysterically (almost weeping) as he watches his own life play out, rather absurdly, on the silver screen. articles.content_zh: 欢迎回来,恶魔们! Blaine Grames, Blake Collier, Caleb Stallings, 我又回到了Spooky Season电影圆桌会议上, 本周我们正观看约翰·卡彭特的"疯狂之口", 这是他第三部"启示录"电影。 因此,请向D行报告,你的座位从我们的座位倒下,紧挨着Sam Neill。 Sam Neil正在倒下爆米花并画出更多的十字架。 让我们有点疯狂吧! Caleb,是什么让你选的? 在疯狂之口? 凯勒布(Caleb):我今年早些时候在看约翰·卡彭特的电影时看过。 这是我从未看过的最后一部电影。 它是一个完美的结束。 一部秋天的,关于作者和恐怖的电影. 就在我的小巷边 比起在秋天的新英格兰小镇 一个不可想象的黑暗大教堂里 还有什么更好的办法去疯狂? 谁不想看电影? 谁不希望他们也遭遇这样的事? Ian:当你这么说的时候... 布莱克(Blake):这次我被特伦特和肯恩的对话深深地打击了,当时肯恩说,“我现在是上帝了......”而特伦特却回应了“我不知道上帝是黑客恐怖作家”这样的大意。 写自己的故事, 更不要说别人的故事了。 只有上帝才能编织叙事,使结局的善良,正义和慈悲得到伸张. 凯勒布: 保持这种理智! 布莱克:没错! 迦勒:如果对耶和华的恐惧是智慧的开始,那么试图篡夺他就是进入了疯狂之口. 伊恩(Ian):的确如此,但对于周围的世界来说,这是一种可能显得疯狂的理智。 这就是特伦特的问题,不是吗? 他听起来很疯狂 但他从假故事中看出 坎恩在编织 布莱克: 我认为这部电影为人类试图编织出关于存在的宏伟故事的失败,以及虚构如何描绘我们自己篡夺上帝的地位和角色的失败,提供了令人惊叹的蓝图。 凯勒布: 这让我想起了蒂姆·凯勒(Tim Keller)讲述了多萝西·赛耶斯(Dorothy Sayers)如何把自己写入她自己的侦探小说中,成为她自己的主角彼得·温西(Peter Wimsey)的某种帮助和救世主. 在"疯狂之口"(The Mouth of Madness)中讲述了相反的故事:萨特·克恩将自己写入他的故事来毁灭他的角色. 布莱克: 因此,通过这种方式,甘恩是撒旦的一种类型... 这意味着但丁的足迹也遍布本片. 布莱恩:*在戈登·拉姆齐的声音*血腥地狱. 伊恩:你知道,我自己也是但丁的适应者。 我们都是生命中的生物, 在一个故事里,像塞耶斯,特勒尔,造物主,成为一个人物。 有许多故事要求权威地解释世界和我们是什么。 Caleb : 多少次提到对Cane书的电影权被选择, 我认为卡彭特在和多少人通过电影媒介 对这些故事很熟悉, 我想现在,30年后,这更真实了。 电影的结局不是在特伦特重读了肯恩的书之后,他才知道这一切的结局,而是在剧院里独自一人,一边吃爆米花一边歇斯底里地取笑(几乎哭泣),一边在银幕上看自己的生活。 布莱克: 在某些方面,将自己交给并非完全出于道德利益的东西是一种混合的道德情感。 我又想起了VVITCH的结局 主角在空中飘来飘去 她的脸既兴奋又被泪水所吓倒 伊恩: 这似乎像疯狂的迷幻 拥抱遗忘。 这是电影的改编, 但这是Reel或TikTok, 所有玩耍的题材都是他们制作的故事的主角 一个减少和贬低

articles.content: Congregations around the world will set aside Sunday, Nov. 1 for the International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church, and this year Open Doors, the Christian ministry that tracks persecution, is asking them to start with Syria. Its 2026 World Watch List moved Syria from 18th place to sixth, a 12-point jump in its score and the largest in the top 10. Open Doors says Syria is now at its most dangerous for Christians since the Islamic State group occupied significant parts of the country. About 300,000 Christians live in Syria. Since the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, the country has been mostly controlled by forces led by Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, an Islamic extremist group with roots in al-Qaeda. The group has made overtures toward moderation and held talks with representatives of Syria’s traditional Christian communities, but it is too soon to know what will come of the new leadership. Widespread instability has produced deadly clashes that have affected Druze and Alawites in particular, with Christians caught in the crossfire, and Islamic State attacks have resumed, including the deadly attack on a church in Damascus in June 2025. “The trauma of what happened hit us all hard,” said “Mourad,” who is responsible for the work of Open Doors’ local partner in Syria. “We thought getting rid of the previous regime would give us some sense of freedom, yet it seems there are still people who only believe in killing.” The interim Syrian constitution adopted in March 2025 makes Islamic law the main source of legislation, and it offers insufficient protection for religious minorities. Pressure on Christians is greatest in Damascus and Aleppo, while the northeast is generally safer. The World Watch List ranks the 50 countries where Christians face the most extreme persecution, using a points system built on data from experts on the ground in 100 countries. North Korea is first with a score of 97 out of 100, followed by Somalia, Yemen, Sudan and Eritrea. Syria is sixth with 90, ahead of Nigeria, Pakistan, Libya and Iran. Open Doors counts more than 388 million Christians worldwide facing high levels of persecution and discrimination for their faith, about one in seven, and in the top 50 countries alone, more than 315 million face very high or extreme persecution. In its 2026 report it recorded 4,849 Christians killed, 4,712 detained and 3,632 churches and Christian properties attacked. For more than 1,600 years Christians have set aside early November to remember believers who suffered for their faith. Open Doors’ free toolkit for churches and small groups includes guided prayer points, videos, sermon material and social images, and this year’s focus is the Middle East, beginning with Syria. Open Doors’ prayer points for Syria ask for three things: that believers would lean on God as their “Rock eternal” (Isaiah 26:4), that converts from Islam would find love and fellowship even when family and friends reject them, and that the victims of the Damascus church attack would feel God’s closeness.

articles.content: Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham told Theo Von on his podcast that nothing a person does or doesn’t do can separate them from God’s love, after Von said he wishes his connection with God were stronger. The conversation is in episode No. 692 of This Past Weekend . Von said his prayer connection with God is the part of his life he likes most, but that when he gets too busy it can feel disconnected. “I wish my connection was stronger,” he said. Cunningham answered, “Dude, I feel you,” and said she was saying it for other people listening too: “There’s nothing that you can or can’t do that’s going to separate you from God’s love and grace and forgiveness. Like that’s why Jesus came and died on the cross because he already knew everything you were going to do.” She added that what comes next is up to the person, who can “educate yourself and read the Bible,” but that “you’re already forgiven.” She also said she feels most connected when she is “prayed up,” a phrase Von said he likes and hears from a friend all the time. Earlier in the conversation, Cunningham said she relies on her faith because of what she does for a living. “You get a lot of hate, you get a lot of praise,” she said. Faith keeps her stable and “who I am,” she said, and she doesn’t care what people’s opinions are about her “because I’m not living for their praise.” Von later asked whether the media is unfair to Christians. Cunningham said that depends on perspective, but that she loves seeing more people say they are believers. “I feel like there’s a revival happening,” she said. She said it can be scary to speak up because people have had bad experiences with church, and that she likes seeing athletes with big platforms be “bold and courageous and come out about Jesus.” Von said more athletes he has gotten to know in the past four years seem to have faith, and that more of his friends are trying to learn about it too. “We want to have some more religious figures on to talk about stuff on here,” he said.

articles.title_zh: “我的上帝需要一点肉汁” ：柯克·富兰克林的新双专辑是他对33年评论家的回答
articles.content: Kirk Franklin’s new album I Am What I Am , his first double album, is out Oct. 30, and he says it is partly an answer to the people who have been questioning his choices for decades. At a listening party in Atlanta , he joked about the whole idea: “I need a little gravy on my God.” The album has 14 songs across two discs, seven studio recordings on the first and seven recorded live on the second. It is Franklin’s 14th studio album, according to the Associated Press, which reports that he is tired of defending his musical decisions. He told the AP he prayed with Chris Brown and Usher before a concert because they asked him to, a moment that drew criticism on social media. “We as believers sometimes become judge and jury,” he said. He also stands by working with GloRilla, whose music is explicit, on the single “This Time.” The song extended his record to 10 No. 1s on Billboard’s Hot Gospel Songs chart, the AP reports. “You start trying to play in other people’s sandboxes, it is going to come with scrutiny,” Franklin said. At the listening party he put it more plainly: “I’ve been trying to explain myself for the last 33 years. This felt like the right opportunity to let people know that I listen and I hear everything that is being said. I am aware. This is my humanity.” Jelly Roll opens the record on “Free Me Tonight,” a spoken-word track the AP says nods to Phil Collins’ “In the Air Tonight.” Franklin reflects on his imperfections and his public criticism on it. Franklin told the AP the song was cathartic and that he once worried it would end his career. “Gospel music is able to handle the raw, unfiltered truth about how ugly and difficult life can be,” he said. On “It Gets Better,” with Tobe Nwigwe, Franklin said at the listening party: “That song was my attempt to find a space to talk about mental health. I’ve had my own journey with anxiety and depression.” He also said, “Living up to the religious standards can create psychological trauma,” and recalled that in his childhood church, young women could be publicly shamed for getting pregnant while the men involved faced no comparable accountability. “Can you imagine the trauma?” he asked. Davido is on “Hope In You,” and Karen Clark Sheard of the Clark Sisters is on the live “Thank You for Everything.” The AP singles out the live “Welcome In,” in which Franklin describes feeling forgotten by God at times while expressing gratitude for God’s steadfast presence. He said the sound of Black church music changed while he was making the album. “The Black church culture changed,” he said. “The church got rid of their choirs and the music was in a space that was not my strength.” Franklin, who is 56 and a 20-time Grammy winner, has no plans to slow down. “The hole that I came from was so deep that whenever I’m around light, I never get tired of feeling the sunlight,” he told the AP.

articles.content: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says the celebration that set off social media after his latest touchdown was a tribute to a gospel song, not a joke about his recent arrest. In the second quarter of the Packers’ 27-19 win over the Carolina Panthers, Jacobs scored on a 1-yard run and briefly put his hands behind his back while teammates congratulated him. Some viewers watching on television thought he was pretending to be handcuffed. Jacobs said he was modeling the moment after a gospel song called “Break Every Chain.” “The guys did it with me,” he said. “I didn’t think it was going to be a thing that can be perceived a certain type of way. But it’s 2026, and it is what it is.” It was Jacobs’ second game of the season. He had spent time on the NFL’s commissioner’s exempt list after charges were filed against him in August over a May altercation with his then-girlfriend, who said he threw her to the ground. Last month he pleaded no contest to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property. He was taken off the list last week and returned to the field, though the league’s investigation is still ongoing. Jacobs said he talked with receiver Savion Williams and other teammates before his season debut, and they planned two celebrations. After his first touchdown of the season, in a 20-17 loss at Detroit, he went to his knees and raised his arms to thank God. The “Break Every Chain” moment was meant for the next one. He also said the broadcast cut away early. “It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that.” The NFL’s investigation of Jacobs remains open.

articles.title_zh: 皮尤： 23至26岁的美国人是该国宗教信仰最少的成年人，而18至22岁的人参加教会的比率高于任何人
articles.content: If you’re 25, the Gen Z church revival you keep hearing about may not describe you. Pew Research Center’s newest report on American religion finds that adults ages 23 to 26 are actually the least religious age group in the country on the core measures it tracks, including how often they pray, how much religion matters to them and whether they identify with a religion. But the group just below them looks very different. Among adults 18 to 22, 41% say they attend a church, synagogue, mosque or other house of worship at least once or twice a month. That is higher than the 33% for the U.S. public as a whole, and higher than adults born in the 1990s, 1980s, 1970s and 1960s. Among adults 23 to 26, the number is 27%, one of the lowest of any age group. Pew calls the overall picture “complicated,” and the report is careful about what the younger figure can carry. Outside of attendance, the youngest adults are less distinctive. They pray and identify with a religion at lower rates than many older groups. They are no more religious than people that age were in 2014, and by Pew’s measures of prayer, religion’s importance and religious identification, both young groups are significantly less religious than their counterparts in 2007. That said, Pew’s sample is small. The 18-to-22 findings rest on 443 respondents from Pew’s 2025 and 2026 surveys, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5.7 percentage points. Applied to the 41% figure, that is a range of roughly 35% to 47%. Split the group by gender or party and the margins widen further. Pew also notes that this has happened before. In its 2014 Religious Landscape Study, 18-to-22-year-olds attended services at a rate 6 points higher than 23-to-26-year-olds. What is new is that the 2025 and 2026 surveys are the first in which the youngest group is significantly more religious than the next group up on all four of Pew’s core indicators. When the youngest adults have looked more religious in the past, Pew says, the effect has tended to fade with time. It adds that the bump may partly reflect a rebound from the pandemic, and that scholars of religion tend to study change over decades. Some of the details cut against the usual storyline about who is showing up. Young men now attend more often than young women, which Pew says it has not seen before, but 35% of the youngest women attend at least monthly, about the same as women born from the 1950s through the 1980s. Among the youngest Republicans, 55% attend monthly. The youngest Democrats also attend at relatively high rates compared with other Democrats, so Pew says it cannot call this an exclusively Republican phenomenon. Across all ages, Pew finds religion holding steady. The shares who identify with a religion, pray daily, call religion very important and attend monthly have been flat since 2020, and 34% of U.S. adults said in a June survey that they had attended services in person in the previous month, the highest since Pew began asking in 2020. Pew says it has no way of knowing whether the youngest adults will follow the old pattern or break it, and describes the open question as “a turning point or a blip.” If it is a revival, it belongs so far to the very youngest adults in the survey.
articles.content_zh: 若你25岁, 皮尤研究中心关于美国宗教的最新报告发现,23-26岁的成年人实际上是该国在追踪的核心衡量标准上最不信奉宗教的年龄组,包括他们的祈祷次数、宗教对他们的重要性以及他们是否认同某一宗教。 但是他们下面的人群看起来很不一样。 在18至22岁的成年人中,41%的人说,他们每月至少去一次或两次教堂、犹太会堂、清真寺或其他礼拜场所。 这比整个美国公众的33%高,也比1990年代,1980年代,1970年代和1960年代出生的成年人高. 在23至26岁的成年人中,这一数字为27%,是任何年龄组中最低的。 皮尤称总体情况“复杂”,报告对年轻人物能够携带什么十分谨慎。 除了出勤外,最年轻的成年人也不太特别. 他们祈祷和认同宗教的比例低于许多老年群体。 他们的宗教程度不比2014年那个年龄的人多,根据皮尤的祈祷、宗教的重要性和宗教认同措施,2007年,这两个青年群体的宗教程度明显低于同龄人。 皮尤的样本很小。 18至22分的调查结果取自皮尤2025年和2026年调查的443个答卷人,误差幅度为上下5.7个百分点。 适用于41%的数字,约为35%至47%。 按性别或政党划分,差额进一步扩大。 Pew也指出,这以前发生过。 在其2014年的"宗教景观研究"中,18至22岁的青少年参加服务,比23至26岁的青少年高6分. 新情况是,2025年和2026年的调查是第一次最年轻的群体比皮尤所有四个核心指标的下一批群体宗教程度高得多。 当最年轻的成年人在过去看起来更加宗教化时,皮尤说,这种效果往往随着时间逐渐消退. 它还说,这一起伏可能部分反映了该流行病的反弹,宗教学者往往研究几十年来的变化。 一些细节与通常的故事情节相对应, 青年男子现在比青年妇女更经常参加,皮尤说以前从未见过这种活动,但最小的妇女中35%至少每月参加,大约与1950年代至1980年代出生的妇女相同。 在最年轻的共和党人中,有55%每月参加. 与其他民主党人相比,最年轻的民主党人也以相对较高的比率参加,因此皮尤称这不能称之为纯粹的共和党现象. 在所有年龄,皮尤发现宗教是稳定的。 认同某种宗教,每日祷告,呼唤宗教非常重要并每月出席的股份自2020年以来一直是平平的,34%的美国成年人在6月的调查中表示,他们上个月曾亲自参加过各种服务,是皮尤自2020年开始询问以来最高的. Pew说,它无法知道最年轻的成年人是否会遵循旧模式或打破旧模式,并形容这个尚未解决的问题是“一个转折点或一滴一滴地”。 如果是复兴,它迄今为止属于调查中最年轻的成年人。

articles.content: 1. At his Substack, Tim Kreider eulogizes the model shops where he dithered in Covid times and the other quirky, abrasive, irreplaceable businesses that are ever more quickly dwindling in Manhattan. There are few things as authentic feeling as genuine indifference to your presence (or antagonism to it). Kreider describes what’s been lost in our frictionless contemporary world: You find the thing you want, you click on it; a day or two later, the thing you wanted arrives. It’s true you don’t have any discomfiting encounters with misanthropes or wackos, but you also don’t come home with any stories. […] The trip to the model shop, including the weird quirks of the owner, used to be as much a part of making a model as sanding or painting it. But for a lot of increasingly timid, introverted consumers, not having to interact with any human beings when they need something is the whole point of the internet. Which is why Jeff Bezos got to rent Venice for his wedding, and one reason people now seem so grotesquely maladjusted to interacting with each other, or living in a society. […] Look: I am as ambivalent as you about Other People. Other People are problematic, impossible. I don’t want to get too sentimentally nostalgic about the lost joys of real-life encounters with crazy, abrasive human beings. I did not enjoy being treated like a contemptible dilettante or a simpleton when all I wanted was to buy some glue. […] But we need the brush and abrasion of Other People, including — maybe even especially — annoying and difficult ones. Because look at the world we’ve constructed to avoid it. If it’s a choice between awkward conversations with eccentrics and cranks or this infinite blank impenetrable wall of corporate contempt we all now face daily — the constant, soul-eroding hassle of creating an account with a unique username and novel password including capital and lowercase letters plus at least one numeral and symbol for every single transaction or errand, scanning a QR code, downloading the app […] accidentally clicking on a popup and scrambling to close the blaring garish page it opens, being asked to take a moment to fill out a brief survey to rate your experience! and Let Them Know How They’re Doing, briefly explain your reason for cancelling, and having to delete one last “We’re Sorry to See You Go!” email — I know which world I choose. Shopping used to be one of the few things that forced us to engage with others, in ways that abrade us but also give to us. Give what? It’s intangible, but maybe just a sense for a reality beyond ourselves. I’m reminded of a quote from Thomas de Zengotita’s brilliantly prophetic Mediated , that “the opposite of real isn’t phony or illusional or fictional — it’s optional.” I think part of what he’s getting at is that anything optional is, once chosen, something that you constructed, something you are responsible for, whose existence depends on your own. What feels real is the thing that exists outside of you — that bracing feeling you get on a mountain or at McSorley’s that the world exists utterly apart from you and will go on existing apart from anything you do. It’s those sorts of encounters, given rather than constructed, arising naturally from a human soul rather than private equity market modeling and focus groups, that seem to get lost in today’s world. Maybe our 2027 NYC Conference will finally be my year for a platza. 2. Apparently CrossFit pioneered the model, common today, of pricey subscriptions to a high-intensity exercise program that function not just for health but as an arena in which one can pursue personal excellence. articles.content: Happy Halloweek, boils and ghouls! Halloween is right around the corner, and so is Michael Myers, back to show everyone why he is the undisputed master slasher! Blaine Grimes, Blake Collier, Caleb Stallings, and I are in our Halloween best and invite you to join us in watching Halloween (2018). Ian : I picked this because it takes me back so vividly to October 2018 and seeing it with my wife, Kristin, and her sister, Anna. Weird as it may sound, this flick lights my heart up like a dozen M-80s in a jack-o’-lantern. I was excited for Michael Myers to return to the big screen and for a new generation to reckon with the horror of The Shape. Caleb : This was the first movie my wife, Aleece, and I ever saw together. Our second date! It’ll always be important to me for that reason alone, but it’s also important to me because it’s a good Halloween sequel! Blake : This movie will forever hold a dear place in my marriage as the first film I took my wife to that caused her to cry and to lose sleep. The first Halloween she watched, she didn’t even bat an eye. This one was just too much for her. Caleb : Wild that we all associate this, for good or for ill, with our wives! Blake : Except Blaine, who just saw it for the first time, right? Blaine : Yeah. I’ve only ever seen the OG and this one. Blake : That is WILD. Caleb : Do you think this one stands out more than others, Ian? Ian : In some significant ways, yes. Halloween (2018) resets the board by proceeding as if there had never been a sequel to the 1978 Halloween . Even titling this film Halloween shows how it positions itself as spiritual successor to the original, and it kind of implicitly announces that nothing with that word and a number after it matters. Caleb : I will admit, I am a sucker for all the various timelines and reboots. But I think this is far and away the best one. Ian : Don’t get me wrong, I enjoy certain sequels before this, but it’s largely in the same way I enjoy the Friday the 13th sequels: schlocky fun. Blake : I don’t hate any of the sequels. But this and its subsequent two films were the first time I felt giddy about being in Haddonfield again. Ian : Halloween (2018) definitely seeks to accomplish something amid its slasher spectacle. I think it wants to go back to basics in showcasing Michael as the evacuated site and vessel of evil: The Shape. Caleb : It’s fascinating how they have to cast the horror of Michael killing five people in 1978 against the larger horror of the subsequent 40 years in American society. Michael isn’t the most prolific serial killer. There have been worse threats than him, but still: he is an avatar of the shapeless Shape of evil. So I think Laurie gets it right later when she talks about how hard and dark the world is. All of us have to be prepared for it. The question is How can we be? Ian : You’re actually approaching something I’m sensing this time around. Although this film officially disavows forty years of sequels, it nevertheless assumes their lore, after a fashion, precisely because the Michael of Halloween (1978) murdered five people, but there’s a mythos to Michael here as though he had carried out everything in those sequels. Caleb : It definitely reckons with its own lore. Laurie’s granddaughter’s friends hear rumors that Laurie was Michael’s sister, which alludes to Halloween 2 (1981). But the truth is much scarier: he’s not related to Laurie at all. His stalking and tormenting her is utterly inscrutable; random. And I think a thesis of this movie is that the world is the same: full of random horror that we can’t ever truly parse out in this life. Michael just happens to be one personification of that. Ian : One of the most satisfying things to me was how the inmates at the asylum chitter and cry out when the mask is presented to Michael, like they sense a power drawing near. That shapeless evil seeks a vessel but also a shape. Michael is at the ready but seeks union with the mask. It’s an anti-wholeness: a complete evac
articles.content_zh: 祝你们万事如意! 万圣节就在拐角处 迈克尔·迈尔斯也在这 向大家展示为什么他是无可争议的刀手! Blaine Grimes Blake Collier Caleb Stallings 我参加万圣节最佳演出 邀请你加入我们观看万圣节(2018年) 伊恩:我选这个是因为它让我生动地回到了2018年10月,并与我的妻子克莉丝汀和她的妹妹安娜一起看到了它. 这个闪光照亮了我的心, 我很兴奋迈克尔·迈尔斯回到大屏幕上 以及新一代人去考虑"形状"的恐怖 凯勒布: 这是我妻子艾莉丝的第一部电影 我曾经一起看过 我们的第二次约会! 但对我来说也很重要, 因为它是一部很好的万圣节续集。 布莱克: 这部电影将永远占据我婚姻中最珍贵的一席之地,作为我带我妻子去看的第一部电影,她因此哭泣并失眠. 她看的第一个万圣节, 这个对她来说太过分了 凯勒布:我们为了好,为了病,为了我们的妻子,把这件事联系起来,真是疯狂! 布莱克:除了布莱恩,谁刚刚第一次看到它,对不对? 对 我只见过OG和这个。 这是WILD。 你觉得这个比其他人更突出吗,伊恩? 伊恩: 在某些重要方面,是的。 万圣节(2018年)通过程序重放板子, 即使授权这部电影万圣节也展示了它如何将自己定位为原作的灵性接班人,它隐含地宣布了这个词和之后的数字都无关紧要. Caleb:我承认,我对各种时限和重回潮流都是个傻瓜。 但我认为这是最远的 Ian:别误会, 之前我还喜欢一些续集, Blake:我不讨厌任何续集。 但是,这及其之后的两部电影,是我第一次对再次出现在哈德顿菲尔德感到迷茫. Ian:万圣节(2018年)肯定在它的刀锋一现中寻求成就。 我认为它想回到基本点 展示迈克尔 被疏散的地点和邪恶的船:形状。 Caleb : 1978年迈克尔杀死了五个人,而美国社会随后的40年却发生了更大的恐怖。 迈克尔并不是最有实力的连环杀手。 曾经有比他更严重的威胁,但仍然:他是一个无形状的邪恶形状的造型. 所以,我想劳里得到它的权利 稍后,当她谈到 多么艰难和黑暗的世界是。 我们所有人都必须为此做好准备。 问题是,我们怎么能这样? (笑声) 伊恩:你实际上正在接近我这次所感知的东西。 虽然这部电影正式否定了40年的续集,但它仍然假定了他们的神话,在时尚化后,正是因为万圣节的迈克尔(1978年)谋杀了五个人,但迈克尔在这里有一个神话,好像他在那些续集中完成了一切。 凯勒布: 它肯定用它自己的神话来考虑 Laurie的孙女朋友听说Laurie是Michael的妹妹, 但事实更可怕:他与劳里根本不相干。 他跟踪和折磨她完全是不可理喻的,是随意的。 我认为这部电影的一个论点是世界是相同的:充满了随机的恐怖,而我们无法在这样的生活中真正地理解。 迈克尔恰好就是个人物 Ian:我最满意的一件事是 当面具被出示给Michael时, 精神病院的囚犯们哭喊着, 好像他们感觉到力量在接近。 这种无形的邪恶既寻求一种容器,也寻求一种形状。 迈克尔已经准备好了,但寻求与面具结合。 这是一个反整齐:一个完整的撤离

articles.content: Five years ago, Laura Lentz had more advice than she wanted. People who had never met her were telling her what to do about her husband, her marriage and her future. “Getting all these opinions and judgments from the outside when no one really knows what’s going on,” she says. “Only the people that are in this know what it takes.” In November 2020, Hillsong founder Brian Houston told staff that Carl Lentz was out at the church’s Manhattan campus, citing breaches of trust. An extramarital affair had come to light. Laura, who had done nothing to land in that spotlight, found herself in it anyway. This month the two of them released a book, Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations To Help Heal the Hurt , and the couple sat down with us to talk about how they got from there to here. “I struggled with a lot of anxiety and just struggling with the opinions of others,” Laura says. “I had to really make sure that didn’t get in here and just remind myself that this is what matters and only we know what’s going on. Lots of therapy has been great. And Jesus, of course, helping through this.” The criticism hasn’t ended, but she says it has changed. “Now I find that’s really gotten quite silent. I think the fruit of our relationship and the fruit of our kids’ lives and where we are now and even writing the book, like you can’t not see God through our story. You can’t not see the miracle through our story.” She is clear about what the book is not. “We’re not out here promoting the book like we’re out to save marriages,” she says. “It’s about me healing, him healing and seeing where that takes us.” The Secrets That Started Small Asked what signs a young married couple should watch for, both of them go to the same place: secrets. “It’s not just big secrets, it’s like the little things,” Laura says. “If you can’t be honest or you’re hiding things from your spouse, those are dangerous and they just compound.” She remembers praying in the weeks before everything surfaced. “I don’t know what it is, but God, you’ve got to get this, just get it out.” Carl says the distance did not begin with the affair. “You don’t start keeping secrets about cheating. You start keeping secrets about fear.” He describes deciding what his wife could handle and keeping the pressure to himself. “It’s when I made the decisions for her on what she was capable of holding,” he says. “Then you stack them and you stack them. By the time you get to the horrific stuff, you’ve already got a pattern of hiding stuff.” What he tells young men now is blunt: get used to being vulnerable with your wife. “It turns out it’s very attractive.” He also rejects the idea that pastors have nobody to tell. “If anybody ever says ‘I didn’t have anybody to be open with,’ I lovingly say I don’t believe you. You chose to not tell anybody.” He says that if he had called Houston on a bad day, he would have been flown out to help. “I did not call. I was not honest. That’s on me.” What Staying Actually Looked Like People tell the spouse who stays that she is brave. Laura is not sure that’s the right word. “It’s so hard to stay, it’s so hard to go,” she says. “Yes, I was brave, I guess, but I was also taking a risk.” She says she would never tell someone to stay in an adulterous relationship, and that she herself saw evidence of change before she did. “There’s gotta be evidence of things that are changing for you to stay and he’s gotta be doing his work.” She describes the early days in small units of time. “We literally went one day at a time. I would wake up and go, okay, I can do today. And that was it.” Carl, a basketball fan, says she has learned the language for it. “Every day, I’m on a one-day contract.
